summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of mental disorders, also called mental illness or psychiatric disorders. It covers how they are defined and classified (DSM, ICD, and dimensional models), the main categories with examples, and their course, disability, and suicide burden. It also summarizes causes such as genetics, prenatal factors, social influences, and drug use, plus diagnostic practice and critiques of psychiatric diagnosis. The text is cut off partway through a discussion of disease mongering.
one_line: Overview of mental disorders covering definitions, classification systems, major categories, causes, outcomes, and critiques of psychiatric diagnosis.
key_facts: A mental disorder, also called a mental illness, mental health condition, or psychiatric disorder, is a behavioral or mental pattern that causes significant distress or impairment of personal functioning.
In 2019, depression affected about 264 million people, dementia about 50 million, bipolar disorder about 45 million, and schizophrenia and other psychoses about 20 million.

The fourth edition of the DSM (DSM-IV), published in 1994, defined a mental disorder as a psychological syndrome or pattern associated with distress, disability, increased risk of death, or significant loss of autonomy.

In 2013, the American Psychiatric Association redefined mental disorders in the DSM-5 as 'a syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in an individual's cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior'.
Edward Shorter, a professor of psychiatry and the history of medicine, wrote How Everyone Became Depressed: The Rise and Fall of the Nervous Breakdown (2013).
There are two widely established systems that classify mental disorders: the DSM and the ICD, which have deliberately converged their codes in recent revisions.

A leading dimensional model is the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, and studies have found two latent factors, internalizing and externalizing disorders, plus a single general factor of psychopathology similar to the g factor for intelligence.
Long-term international studies of schizophrenia found that over half of individuals recover in terms of symptoms, and around a fifth to a third recover in terms of symptoms and functioning.
A follow-up study by Tohen and coworkers found that around half of people initially diagnosed with bipolar disorder achieve symptomatic recovery within six weeks, and nearly all within two years.
Unipolar (Major) depressive disorder is the third leading cause of disability worldwide, of any condition mental or physical, accounting for 65.5 million years lost.
Suicide is a leading cause of death among teenagers and adults under 35, with an estimated 10 to 20 million non-fatal attempted suicides every year worldwide.

Statistical research on eleven disorders found that people with schizophrenia or ADHD are seven times more likely to have affected partners with the same disorder, and people with autism spectrum disorders are 10 times more likely to have a spouse with the same disorder.
Since the 1980s, Paula Caplan has been concerned about the subjectivity of psychiatric diagnosis and people being arbitrarily 'slapped with a psychiatric label'.

In 2013, psychiatrist Allen Frances wrote 'The New Crisis of Confidence in Psychiatric Diagnosis', arguing that psychiatric diagnosis 'still relies exclusively on fallible subjective judgments rather than objective biological tests'.

entities.name: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders
entities.role: Standard classification manual for mental disorders; DSM-IV (1994) and DSM-5 (2013) are discussed, and it is one of two widely established classification systems.

entities.name: International Classification of Diseases
entities.role: Classification system for mental disorders, referred to as ICD; the final draft of ICD-11 contains a definition very similar to DSM-5's.

entities.name: American Psychiatric Association
entities.role: Publisher of the DSM; redefined mental disorders in the DSM-5 in 2013.

entities.name: Edward Shorter
entities.role: Professor of psychiatry and the history of medicine who wrote How Everyone Became Depressed (2013).

entities.name: Paula Caplan
entities.role: Critic who has been concerned since the 1980s about the subjectivity of psychiatric diagnosis.

entities.name: Allen Frances
entities.role: Psychiatrist who wrote the 2013 paper 'The New Crisis of Confidence in Psychiatric Diagnosis' and was concerned about overdiagnosis.

entities.name: Tohen
entities.role: Researcher whose follow-up study found symptomatic recovery in people initially diagnosed with bipolar disorder.

entities.name: World Health Organization
entities.role: Concluded that long-term schizophrenia studies relieved patients and clinicians of the chronicity paradigm.

entities.name: Peter Breggin
entities.role: Marginalized psychiatrist cited as accusing psychiatry of systematic medicalization of normality.

entities.name: Thomas Szasz
entities.role: Marginalized psychiatrist cited as accusing psychiatry of systematic medicalization of normality.

entities.name: Stuart A. Kirk
entities.role: Outside critic cited as accusing psychiatry of systematic medicalization of normality.

entities.name: Robert Spitzer
entities.role: Insider who worked for and promoted the American Psychiatric Association and has raised concerns about psychiatric diagnosis.

entities.name: Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology
entities.role: Described as a leading dimensional model of mental disorders.

entities.name: Chinese Classification of Mental Disorders
entities.role: Classification scheme that may be used in non-western cultures.

entities.name: Psychodynamic Diagnostic Manual
entities.role: Manual that may be used by those of alternative theoretical persuasions.

entities.name: British Medical Journal
entities.role: Journal whose 2002 editorial warned of inappropriate medicalization leading to disease mongering.
